claims.text: The alloy is initially a chemically disordered, homogeneous single-phase material.
The initial alloy has no detectable superconductivity at ambient or moderately low temperatures.
Extreme chemical disorder generates local lattice distortions and atomic-scale strain fields in the alloy.
Chemical complexity produces significant local variations in atomic mass and bonding.
Local lattice distortions and variations in mass and bonding soften specific phonon modes.
The softened phonon modes enhance electron-phonon coupling.
Enhanced electron-phonon coupling can overcome the effects of disorder-induced scattering in this alloy.
The enhanced electron-phonon coupling stabilizes a low-temperature superconducting condensate through Cooper-pair formation.
Cooling below a critical temperature will produce a sharp transition to zero electrical resistance.
Cooling below the critical temperature will open a superconducting energy gap detectable by tunneling spectroscopy.
The superconducting state will exhibit a diamagnetic susceptibility response.
Above the critical temperature, the alloy will display metallic behavior with finite resistance.
Above the critical temperature, the alloy will have no superconducting energy gap.
The proposed mechanism applies only while the alloy retains a uniform, disordered, single-phase structure.
Phase segregation, impurity phases, or dominant extrinsic defects may suppress or mask the electron-phonon interactions required by the hypothesis.
Disorder-induced scattering may limit the superconducting state despite any enhancement of electron-phonon coupling.
